per_finding.note: Grounded: computed_lr derives directly from byte-anchored pooled sensitivity (0.97) and specificity (0.41) from the Blood Advances 2020 meta-analysis (34 studies, 22,849 patients), confirmed identical for the highly sensitive ELISA (Vidas) subgroup matching this finding's assay description. LR+ = 0.97/0.59 = 1.64 — a WEAK positive likelihood ratio. This is the clinically correct result: an elevated D-dimer barely shifts post-test probability upward (e.g., from a 20.4% pretest prevalence, odds 0.256 x 1.64 = 0.42, post-test ~30%). D-dimer is a RULE-OUT test; its diagnostic power lives in LR- = (1-0.97)/0.41 = 0.073, where a negative result drives PE probability very low. The expected metric for THIS positive finding (LR+) is therefore inherently unimpressive — the test was not designed to rule PE in. Pretest prevalence (~0.20) anchored to the Christopher study (van Belle 2006 JAMA, 3306 suspected-PE patients). Cochrane Crawford 2016 (CD010864) corroborates direction (sensitivity 80-100%, specificity 23-63%) but its abstract reports only ranges, so the Blood Advances pooled point estimates are the stronger primary source used for computation.

per_finding.note: Finding f2 = D-dimer below assay cutoff (negative), expected metric LR-, fully grounded. Primary source is the ASH-guideline Blood Advances 2020 test-accuracy meta-analysis (Patel/Lim/Le Gal et al.; 34 studies, 22,849 suspected-PE patients), which byte-anchors pooled sensitivity 0.97 (0.96-0.98) and specificity 0.41 (0.36-0.46). Corroborated by the Crawford 2016 Cochrane review (CD010864), which reports sensitivity ranges 80-100% and specificity 23-63% across studies, and by an independently reported pooled LR- of 0.17 (0.13-0.23) in another analysis (our 0.073 uses the highest-quality 34-study pooled sens/spec). Note: D-dimer is highly sensitive but poorly specific, so it functions only as a rule-out test (good LR-), not a rule-in test; specificity falls further in elderly patients, motivating age-adjusted cutoffs. per_finding.lr_formula: The Wells 'clinical signs of DVT' criterion is leg swelling PLUS pain on deep-vein palpation. West/Goodacre 2007 report these as already-pooled positive likelihood ratios (LR+ used directly as published, no sens/spec recomputation needed): leg swelling LR+ = 2.11, leg pain LR+ = 1.60, current DVT LR+ = 2.05, thrombophlebitis LR+ = 2.20. Taking leg swelling (the dominant objective sign of the criterion) as the representative value => computed_lr = 2.11. Prior: PE prevalence in suspected-PE workup population ~= 0.20 (Christopher study, JAMA 2006). Post-test odds shift example: pretest odds 0.20/0.80 = 0.25; x LR 2.11 = 0.528 post-test odds => post-test prob ~= 0.35.
per_finding.note: Grounded in West, Goodacre & Sampson 2007 QJM (PMID 18089542), a systematic review/meta-analysis of 18 studies / 5997 suspected-PE patients reporting pooled positive likelihood ratios for individual clinical features. The Wells 'clinical signs of DVT' criterion (leg swelling + pain on deep-vein palpation) maps to leg swelling LR+ 2.11 and leg pain LR+ 1.60 (closely corroborated by current DVT 2.05 and thrombophlebitis 2.20). computed_lr=2.11 uses the literal published LR+ for leg swelling as the representative quantity (LR used directly, not derived from sens/spec). Note the expected metric was OR_or_LR; the meta-analysis publishes LRs directly, so no OR conversion was needed. Lucassen 2011 (the suggested anchor) pools whole decision rules, not individual items, so it could not ground a per-item number; West/Goodacre 2007 is the correct primary source for individual-sign test characteristics. The author's own caveat: individual clinical features 'only slightly altered the probability' of PE and had little diagnostic value in isolation, with significant between-study heterogeneity — so the direction (positive sign raises PE probability) is solid but the precise magnitude should be used cautiously. PE workup prevalence prior ~0.20 from Christopher study (JAMA 2006).

per_finding.note: Primary data byte-anchored to Marchick/Kline et al., Ann Emerg Med 2010 (PMID 19766353), a prospective multicenter ED cohort of 6,049 patients (354 PE). The study reports tachycardia (HR>100/min) frequencies of 28.8% (PE) vs 15.7% (non-PE) and a DIRECTLY published positive likelihood ratio of 1.8 (95% CI 1.5-2.2). I independently recomputed LR+ from the two frequencies as 0.288/0.157=1.83, which reproduces the published 1.8, so the number is fully grounded in primary frequencies. Direction is positive (tachycardia raises PE odds), consistent with its inclusion as a Wells/PERC criterion. Note: sensitivity here (28.8%) is the fraction of PE patients who are tachycardic in this cohort, not a formal diagnostic sensitivity; LR+ 1.8 indicates a weak-to-moderate positive predictor. For the PE pretest prior, the standard suspected-PE workup prevalence is ~0.20 (Christopher study, JAMA 2006), higher than this particular ED ECG cohort's 5.9%; applying LR+ 1.8 to a 0.20 prior gives post-test probability ~0.31 (odds 0.25*1.8=0.45 -> p=0.31).

per_finding.note: DIRECTION + MAGNITUDE GROUNDED, WITH A CAVEAT ON FORM. The finding maps to the Wells item 'immobilization >=3 days or surgery within 4 weeks' (1.5 Wells points). No landmark study reports a clean sensitivity/specificity for this individual item in isolation (Lucassen 2011 and PIOPED II report rules as a whole or unadjusted prevalences). The cleanest primary diagnostic quantity for the surgery/immobilization criterion is the multivariable logistic-regression weight in the Revised Geneva Score derivation (Le Gal 2006, n=965 suspected-PE patients, PE prevalence 23.0%): coefficient 0.78 for 'surgery or fracture within 1 month' => adjusted OR exp(0.78) = 2.18. Per the procedure, an adjusted OR for a clinical criterion is used as the LR proxy; computed_lr = 2.18. CAVEATS: (1) The published value is the log-odds COEFFICIENT; the OR (2.18) is derived by exponentiation, and the 95% CI is NOT printed in the paper, so the point estimate is byte-anchored but its precision is not. (2) The Geneva item is 'surgery or fracture within 1 month' (general-anesthesia surgery / lower-limb fracture) and does not include the '>=3 days immobilization' clause that the Wells item adds — so it is a close but not identical operationalization; the Wells immobilization+surgery composite would likely carry a similar or slightly larger OR. (3) An alternative anchor, the prognostic OR 2.2 (95% CI 1.8-2.7, Nauffal/Monreal JTH 2012), is for MORTALITY among confirmed-PE patients, NOT diagnostic discrimination, and was deliberately NOT used. PRIOR: PE prevalence in the suspected-PE workup population = 0.204 (674/3306, Christopher Study, JAMA 2006), ~0.20. Note the near-coincidence: the diagnostic OR proxy 2.18 and the unrelated mortality OR 2.2 are numerically almost identical despite measuring different things; the value reported here is the diagnostic one.

per_finding.note: Grounded in PIOPED II (Stein 2006 NEJM), the landmark study establishing CTPA test characteristics and effectively the diagnostic reference standard for PE. CTA-alone sensitivity 83% (150/181) and specificity 96% (567/592) are byte-anchored from the NEJM paper (confirmed in the original abstract via PubMed 16738268 and re-quoted with raw counts in the ERS Breathe review PMC10928556). LR+ = 0.83/0.04 = 20.75 — a very high positive likelihood ratio, consistent with a confirmatory test. Caveats: (1) Performance is location-dependent — sensitivity 97% main/lobar, 68% segmental, 25% subsegmental — so the pooled LR+ understates main-vessel and overstates subsegmental performance. (2) PPV varied with pretest probability (96% with concordant high/low clinical assessment vs 58% with low pretest probability), reflecting the standard LR-independent dependence of post-test probability on prior; PE workup prevalence in the suspected-PE population is roughly 0.15-0.23 (~0.20). (3) An alternative LR+ using the 96% specificity rounded differently changes little; using exact counts spec = 567/592 = 0.9578 gives LR+ = 0.829/0.0422 = 19.6, so the reported value is robust at ~20.

per_finding.note: A negative CTPA on an adequate (diagnostic-quality) study is the index finding; the expected metric is LR-. Computed directly from PIOPED II (Stein 2006 NEJM, PMID 16738268) sensitivity 83% and specificity 96%: LR- = (1-0.83)/0.96 = 0.18. This is byte-anchored to the literal abstract sentence. Corroboration: PIOPED II reported the negative predictive value of a negative CTA as 96%, 89%, and 60% for low, intermediate, and high Wells clinical probability respectively (WikiJournalClub summary), confirming that a negative CTPA strongly but not perfectly lowers PE probability and that with high pretest probability a negative CTPA alone may be insufficient (concordance principle). Caveat: 83% sensitivity (CTA alone) reflects 2006 multidetector technology and a composite reference standard; modern CTPA scanners likely have higher sensitivity, so the true LR- in current practice may be somewhat lower (more strongly exclusionary). Management studies (e.g., Christopher 2006 JAMA and a 23-study meta-analysis) report ~1.2-1.4% 3-month VTE risk after a negative CTPA, consistent with this LR- producing a low post-test probability in the typical workup population (PE prevalence ~20%).
